installation.note: gzip is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The gzip command compresses files using the gzip compression algorithm, replacing the original file with a compressed version that has a .gz extension. It's one of the most common compression tools on Linux, providing good compression ratios and fast compression/decompression speeds.
when_to_use: Compress files to save disk space
Reduce file sizes for faster transfers

syntax.description: Compress one or more files. By default, gzip replaces the original file with a compressed .gz version. If no files are specified, gzip reads from stdin.

options.use_case: Extract compressed files, alternative to gunzip command
Compress files while keeping the original (creates file.txt.gz, keeps file.txt)
Compress all files in a directory and subdirectories
Balance between speed (-1) and compression ratio (-9)
See compression ratio and file size reduction
Verify compressed files are not corrupted

misconceptions.title: gzip creates archives
misconceptions.misconception: gzip can compress multiple files into a single archive
misconceptions.reality: gzip compresses individual files. To compress multiple files into one archive, use tar first: tar -czf archive.tar.gz files/
misconceptions.tip: Use 'tar -czf' to create compressed archives of multiple files or directories

misconceptions.title: gzip preserves original by default
misconceptions.misconception: gzip keeps the original file after compression
misconceptions.reality: gzip removes the original file by default. Use -k flag to keep the original file.
misconceptions.tip: Always use -k if you need to keep the original file: gzip -k file.txt

common_pitfalls.description: Forgetting -k flag causes original files to be deleted
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -k flag when you need to keep originals, or backup files before compression

common_pitfalls.description: Compressing .gz, .zip, or image files provides little benefit and wastes time
common_pitfalls.solution: Don't compress files that are already compressed (images, videos, archives)

common_pitfalls.description: gzip file.txt works, but gzip directory/ doesn't compress the directory itself
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -r for recursive compression of files in directories, or use tar -czf for directory archives

related_commands.relationship: Decompression; gunzip is equivalent to gzip -d
Archiving; often used with gzip to create compressed archives
Alternative compression; zip creates .zip archives, gzip creates .gz files

best_practices: Use -k to keep original files when needed: gzip -k file.txt
Use -9 for maximum compression when space matters, -1 for speed
Use -v to see compression statistics and verify results
Combine with tar for multi-file archives: tar -czf archive.tar.gz directory/
Test compressed files with -t to verify integrity
performance_tips: Level 1 is fastest but creates larger files, level 9 is slowest but smallest
Default level 6 provides good balance between speed and compression
Text files compress much better than binary files
Already compressed files (images, videos) won't compress further

additional_notes.file_replacement: By default, original files are replaced. Use -k to keep originals.
additional_notes.archive_format: gzip compresses individual files. For archives, use tar with gzip.
additional_notes.decompression: gzip -d and gunzip are equivalent - both decompress .gz files
